The defective writing is like, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, בּטח, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.7">Psa 112:7</reference>, and gives no authority to prefer דּבּר = מדבּר (Böttcher). That דּברי, corresponding to the plur. תּפּוּחי, is not used, arises from this, that דבר is here manifestly not a word without connection, but a sentence of motive, contents, and aim united. For על־אפניו, the meaning of בּעתּו presents itself from <reference osisRef="Prov.15.23">Pro 15:23</reference>, according to which, among the old interpreters, Symmachus, Jerome, and Luther render “at its time.” Abulwalîd compared the Arab. âiffan (âibban, also 'iffan, whence 'aly 'iffanihi, <hi type="italic">justo tempore</hi>), which, as Orelli has shown in his <hi type="italic">Synon. der Zeitbegriffe</hi>, p. 21f., comes from the roots af ab, to drive (from within) going out, time as consisting of individual moments, the one of which drives on the other, and thus denotes time as a course of succession. One may not hesitate as to the prep. על, for אפנים would, like עתּות, denote the circumstances, the relations of the time, and על would, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, in על־פּי and על־דּברתי, have the meaning of κατά. But the form אפניו, which like חפניו, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.12">Lev 16:12</reference>, sounds dualistic, appears to oppose this. Hitzig supposes that אפנים may designate the time as a circle, with reference to the two arches projecting in opposite directions, but uniting themselves together; but the circle which time describes runs out from one point, and, moreover, the Arab. names for time âfaf, âifaf, and the like, which interchange with âiffan, show that this does not proceed from the idea of circular motion. Ewald and others take for אפניו the meaning of wheels (the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., after Kimchi, ἐπὶ τῶν τροχῶν αὐτῆς), whereby the form is to be interpreted as dual of אפן = אופן, “a word driven on its wheels,” - so Ewald explains: as the potter quickly and neatly forms a vessel on his wheels, thus a fit and quickly framed word. But דבר signifies to drive cattle and to speak = to cause words to follow one another (cf. Arab. syâḳ, pressing on = flow of words), but not to drive = to fashion in that artisan sense. Otherwise Böttcher, “a word fitly spoken, a pair of wheels perfect in their motion,” to which he compares the common people “in their jesting,” and adduces all kinds of heterogeneous things partly already rejected by Orelli (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the Homeric ἐπιτροχάδην, which is certainly no commendation). But “jesting” is not appropriate here; for what man conceives of human speech as a carriage, one only sometimes compares that of a babbler to a sledge, or says of him that he shoves the cart into the mud.<note placement="foot">It is something different when the weaver’s beam, minwâl in Arab., is metaph. for kind and manner: they are 'aly minwâl wâḥad, is equivalent to they are of a like calibre, Arab. kalib, which is derived from καλόπους (καλοπόδιον), a shoemaker’s last.</note> <div eID="gen11635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11636" type="x-p"/> Is it then thus decided that אפניו is a dual? It may be also like אשׂריו, the plur. especially in the adverbial expression before us, which readily carried the abbreviation with it (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Gesen. <hi type="italic">Lehrgebr</hi>. §134, Anm. 17). On this supposition, Orelli interprets אפן from אפן, to turn, in the sense of turning about, circumstances, and reminds of this, that in the post-bibl. Heb. this word is used as indefinitely as τρόπος, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, באופן מה, <hi type="italic">quodammodo</hi> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Reland’s <hi type="italic">Analecta Rabbinica</hi>, 1723, p. 126). This late Talm. usage of the word can, indeed, signify nothing as to the bibl. word; but that אפנים, abbreviated אפנים, can mean circumstances, is warranted by the synon. אודות. Aquila and Theodotion appear to have thus understood it, for their ἐπὶ ἁρμόζουσιν αὐτῷ, which they substitute for the colourless οὕτως of the lxx, signifies: under the circumstances, in accordance therewith. So Orelli thus rightly defines: “אפנים denote the âḥwâl, circumstances and conditions, as they form themselves in each turning of time, and those which are ascribed to דבר by the suffix are those to which it is proper, and to which it fits in. Consequently a word is commended which is spoken whenever the precise time arrives to which it is adapted, a word which is thus spoken at its time as well as at its place (van Dyk, fay mahllah), and the grace of which is thereby heightened.” Aben Ezra’s explanation, על פנים הראויים, in the approved way, follows the opinion of Abulwalîd and Parchon, that אפניו is equivalent to פניו (cf. aly wajhihi, <hi type="italic">sua ratione</hi>), which is only so far true, that both words are derived from R. פן, to turn. In the figure, it is questionable whether by תּפּוּחי זהב, apples of gold, or gold-coloured apples, are meant (Luther: as pomegranates and citrons); thus oranges are meant, as at Zec 4:12. הזּהב denotes golden oil. Since כסף, besides, signifies a metallic substance, one appears to be under the necessity of thinking of apples of gold; cf. the brazen pomegranates. But (1) apples of gold of natural size and massiveness are obviously too great to make it probable that such artistic productions are meant; (2) the material of the emblem is usually not of less value than that of which it is the emblem (Fleischer); (3) the Scriptures are fond of comparing words with flowers and fruits, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.31">Pro 10:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.12.14">Pro 12:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.13.2">Pro 13:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.18.20">Pro 18:20</reference>, and to the essence of the word which is rooted in the spirit, and buds and grows up to maturity through the mouth and the lips, the comparison with natural fruits corresponds better in any case than with artificial. Thus, then, we interpret “golden apples” as the poetic name for oranges, <hi type="italic">aurea mala</hi>, the Indian name of which with reference to <hi type="italic">or</hi> (gold) was changed into the French name <hi type="italic">orange</hi>, as our <hi type="italic">pomeranze</hi> is equivalent to <hi type="italic">pomum aurantium</hi>. משׂכּיּות is the plur. of משׂכּית, already explained, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.11">Pro 18:11</reference>; the word is connected neither with שׂכך, to twist, wreathe (Ewald, with most Jewish interpreters)<note placement="foot">On this proceeds also the beautiful interpretation by Maimuni in the preface to <hi type="italic">More Nebuchim</hi>: <hi type="italic">Maskiyyôth sont des ciselures réticulaires</hi>, etc., according to Munk’s translation from the Arab. text, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Kohut’s <hi type="italic">Pers. Pentateuch-Uebers</hi>. (1871), p. 356. Accordingly Jewish interpreters (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Elia Wilna) understand under אפניו the four kinds of writing: פשׁט, רמז, דרושׁ, and סוד, which are comprehended under the memorial word פרדס.</note> nor with שׂכה, to pierce, <hi type="italic">infigere</hi> (Redslob, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Ps.73.7">Psa 73:7</reference>); it signifies medal or ornament, from שׂכה, to behold (cf. שׂכיּה, θέα = θέαμα, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.6">Isa 2:6</reference>), here a vessel which is a delight to the eyes. In general the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. rightly, ἐν μορφώμασιν ἀργύρου; Symmachus and Theodotion, more in accordance with the fundamental idea, ἐν περιβλέπτοις ἀργύρου; the Syr. and Targ. specially: in vessels of embossed work (נגוּדי, from נגד, to draw, to extend); yet more specially the lxx, ἐν ὁρμίσκῳ σαρδίου, on a chain of cornelian stone, for which, perhaps, ἐν φορμίσκῳ (Jäger) ἀργυρίου, in a little silver basket, is the original phrase. Aquila, after <hi type="italic">Bereschith rabba c</hi>. 93, translates by μῆλα χρύσου ἐν δίσκοις ἀργυφίου. Jerome: <hi type="italic">in lectis argenteis</hi>, appears to have fallen into the error of taking משב for משכב, <hi type="italic">lectus</hi>. Hitzig here emends a self-made ἅπαξ λεγ. Luther’s “golden apples in silver baskets” is to be preferred.<note placement="foot">A favourite expression of Goethe’s, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Büchmann’s <hi type="italic">Geflügelte Worte</hi>, 1688.</note> <div eID="gen11636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11637" type="x-p"/> A piece of sculpture which represents fruit by golden little disks or points within groups of leaves is not meant - for the proverb does not speak of such pretty little apples - but golden oranges are meant. A word in accordance with the circumstances which occasion it, is like golden oranges which are handed round in silver salvers or on silver waiters. Such a word is, as adopting another figure we might say, like a well-executed picture, and the situation into which it appropriately fits is like its elegant frame. The comparison with fruit is, however, more significant; it designates the right word as a delightful gift, in a way which heightens its impression and its influences.
entries.57be581062797be7aa33f8ecf9cc1691d9abb535: <reference osisRef="Prov.25.12">Pro 25:12</reference> <div eID="gen11637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11638" type="x-p"/> Another proverb continues the commendation of the effective word; for it represents, in emblem, the interchangeable relation of speaker and hearer: <div eID="gen11638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11639" type="x-p"/> A golden earring and an ornament of fine gold - <div eID="gen11639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11640" type="x-p"/> A wise preacher to an ear that heareth;<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, as the former two ornaments form a beautiful <hi type="italic">ensemble</hi>, so the latter two, the wise preacher of morality and an attentive ear, form a harmonious whole: על, down upon, is explained by Deu 32:2. נזם, at <reference osisRef="Prov.11.12">Pro 11:12</reference>, standing along with באף, meant a ring for the nose; but here, as elsewhere, it means an earring (lxx, Jerome, <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>.), translated by the Syr. and Targ. by קדשׁא, because it serves as a talisman. A ring for the nose<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Gieger’s <hi type="italic">Zeitschrift</hi>, 1872, pp. 45-48, where it is endeavoured to be shown that נזם, as an earring, is rejected from the later biblical literature, because it had become “an object used in the worship of idols,” and that the word was used only of a ring for the nose as a permissible ornament, while עגיל was used for the earring. But that does not apply to the Solomonic era; for that, in the passage under review, נזם signifies a ring for the nose, is only a supposition of Geiger’s, because it accords with his construction of history.</note> cannot also be here thought of, because this ornament is an emblem of the attentive ear: willingly accepted chastisement or instruction is an ear-ornament to him who hears (Stier). But the gift of the wise preacher, which consists in rightly dividing the word of truth, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.15">2Ti 2:15</reference>, is as an ornament for the neck or the breast חלי (= Arab. khaly, fem. חליה = ḥilyt), of fine gold (כּתם, jewel, then particularly precious gold, from כּתם, Arab. katam, <hi type="italic">recondere</hi>).<note placement="foot">Hitzig compares Arab. kumêt; but this means bayard, as Lagarde remarks, the Greek κόμαιθος; and if by כתם gold foxes (gold money) are to be thought of, yet they have nothing whatever to do with bayards (red-brown horses); cf. Beohmer, <hi type="italic">de colorum nominibus equinorum</hi>, in his <hi type="italic">Roman. Stud</hi>. Heft 2, 1872, p. 285.</note> <div eID="gen11640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11641" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. well: κόσμος ἀπυροχρύσου (fine gold); on the contrary (perhaps in want of another name for gold), כתם is translated, by the lxx and Syr., by sardine; by the Targ., by emerald; and by Jerome, by <hi type="italic">margaritum</hi>.<note placement="foot">Another Greek translates πίνωσις χρυσῆ. This πίνωσις is a philological mystery, the solution of which has been attempted by Bochart, Letronne, and Field.</note> <div eID="gen11641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11642" type="x-p"/> It looks well when two stand together, the one of whom has golden earrings, and the other wears a yet more precious golden necklace - such a beautiful mutual relationship is formed by a wise speaker and a hearer who listens to his admonitions.
entries.e69b41888cef8f342e0a395efedfe39334e653b2: <reference osisRef="Prov.25.13">Pro 25:13</reference> <div eID="gen11642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11643" type="x-p"/> The following comparative tristich refers to faithful service rendered by words: <div eID="gen11643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11644" type="x-p"/> Like the coolness of snow on a harvest day <div eID="gen11644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11645" type="x-p"/> Is a faithful messenger to them that send him: <div eID="gen11645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11646" type="x-p"/> He refresheth the soul of his master. <div eID="gen11646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11647" type="x-p"/> The coolness (צנּה from צנן, צנן, to be cool) of snow is not that of a fall of snow, which in the time of harvest would be a calamity, but of drink cooled with snow, which was brought from Lebanon or elsewhere, from the clefts of the rocks; the peasants of Damascus store up the winter’s snow in a cleft of the mountains, and convey it in the warm months to Damascus and the coast towns. Such a refreshment is a faithful messenger (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding ציר, <reference osisRef="Prov.13.17">Pro 13:17</reference>, here following קציר as a kind of echo) to them that send him (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding this plur. at <reference osisRef="Prov.10.26">Pro 10:26</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.22.21">Pro 22:21</reference>); he refreshes, namely (ו <hi type="italic">explicativum</hi>, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.19">Eze 18:19</reference>, <hi type="italic">etenim filius</hi>, like the ו <hi type="italic">et quidem</hi>, Mal 1:11, different from the ו of conditional clause <reference osisRef="Prov.23.3">Pro 23:3</reference>), the soul of his master; for the answer which he brings to his master refreshes him, as does a drink of snow-cooled water on a hot harvest day.
entries.beced136abf8b2520bdc51abee258c711709b327: <reference osisRef="Prov.25.14">Pro 25:14</reference> <div eID="gen11647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11648" type="x-p"/> This proverb relates to the word which promises much, but remains unaccomplished: <div eID="gen11648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11649" type="x-p"/> Clouds and wind, and yet no rain - <div eID="gen11649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11650" type="x-p"/> A man who boasteth with a false gift. <div eID="gen11650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11651" type="x-p"/> Incorrectly the lxx and Targ. refer the predicate contained in the concluding word of the first line to all the three subjects; and equally incorrectly Hitzig, with Heidenheim, interprets מתּת שׁקר, of a gift that has been received of which one boasts, although it is in reality of no value, because by a lying promise a gift is not at all obtained. But as לחם כזבים, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.3">Pro 23:3</reference>, is bread which, as it were, deceives him who eats it, so מתת שׁקר is a gift which amounts to a lie, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, a deceitful pretence. Rightly Jerome: <hi type="italic">vir gloriosus et promissa non complens</hi>. In the Arab. ṣaliḍ, which Fleischer compares, the figure 14a and its counterpart 14b are amalgamated, for this word signifies both a boaster and a cloud, which is, as it were, boastful, which thunders much, but rains only sparsely or not at all. Similar is the Arab. khullab, clouds which send forth lightning, and which thunder, but yet give no rain; we say to one, <hi type="italic">magno promissor hiatu</hi>: thou art (Arab.) kabaraḳn khullabin, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, as Lane translates it: “Thou art only like lightning with which is no rain.” Schultens refers to this proverbial Arabic, <hi type="italic">fulmen nubis infecundae</hi>. Liberality is called (Arab.) nadnay, as a watering, cf. Pro 11:25. The proverb belongs to this circle of figures. It is a saying of the German peasants, “<hi type="italic">Wenn es sich wolket, so will es regnen</hi>” [when it is cloudy, then there will be rain]; but according to another saying, “<hi type="italic">nicht alle Wolken regnen</hi>” [it is not every cloud that yields rain]. “There are clouds and wind without rain.”
entries.a5c54a21167101e6ca5be64c9bbc6d5149d7920c: <reference osisRef="Prov.25.15">Pro 25:15</reference> <div eID="gen11651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11652" type="x-p"/> Three proverbs follow, which have this in common, that they exhort to moderation: 15 By forbearance is a judge won over,      And a gentle tongue breaketh the bone. קצין (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.6.7">Pro 6:7</reference>) does not denote any kind of distinguished person, but a judge or a person occupying a high official position. And פּתּה does not here mean, to talk over or delude; but, like <reference osisRef="Jer.20.7">Jer 20:7</reference>, to persuade, to win over, to make favourable to one; for ארך אפּים (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.14.29">Pro 14:29</reference>) is dispassionate calmness, not breaking out into wrath, which finally makes it manifest that he who has become the object of accusation, suspicion, or of disgrace, is one who nevertheless has right on his side; for indecent, boisterous passion injures even a just cause; while, on the contrary, a quiet, composed, thoughtful behaviour, which is not embarrassed by injustice, either experienced or threatened, in the end secures a decision in our favour. “Patience overcomes” is an old saying. The soft, gentle tongue (cf. רך, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.1">Pro 15:1</reference>) is the opposite of a passionate, sharp, coarse one, which only the more increases the resistance which it seeks to overcome. “Patience,” says a German proverb, “breaks iron;” another says, “Patience is stronger than a diamond.” So here: a gentle tongue breaketh the bone (גּרם = עצם, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.17.22">Pro 17:22</reference>), it softens and breaks to pieces that which is hardest. Sudden anger makes the evil still worse; long-suffering, on the contrary, operates convincingly; cutting, immoderate language, embitters and drives away; gentle words, on the contrary, persuade, if not immediately, yet by this, that they remain as it were unchangeable.
entries.ceb1ce1fb36f7dd9f66cf662bf8de43528be46ee: <reference osisRef="Prov.25.16">Pro 25:16</reference> <div eID="gen11652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11653" type="x-p"/> Another way of showing self-control: <div eID="gen11653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11654" type="x-p"/> Hast thou found honey? eat thy enough, <div eID="gen11654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11655" type="x-p"/> Lest thou be surfeited with it, and vomit it up. <div eID="gen11655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11656" type="x-p"/> Honey is pleasant, salutary, and thus to be eaten sparingly, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.13">Pro 24:13</reference>, but <hi type="italic">ne quid nimis</hi>. Too much is unwholesome, 27a: αὐτοῦ καὶ μέλιτος τὸ πλέον ἐστὶ χολή, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, even honey enjoyed immoderately is as bitter as gall; or, as Freidank says: <hi type="italic">des honges süeze erdruizet sô mans ze viel geniuzet</hi> [the sweetness of honey offends when one partakes too much of it]. Eat if thou hast found any in the forest or the mountains, דּיּךּ, thy enough (lxx τὸ ἱκανόν; the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. τὸ ἀρκοῦν σοι), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, as much as appeases thine appetite, that thou mayest not become surfeited and vomit it out (והקאתו with <hi type="italic">Tsere</hi>, and א quiesc., as at <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.10">2Sa 14:10</reference>; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 116a, and Parchon under קוא). Fleischer, Ewald, Hitzig, and others, place <reference osisRef="Prov.25.16">Pro 25:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.25.17">Pro 25:17</reference> together, so as to form an emblematic tetrastich; but he who is surfeited is certainly, in <reference osisRef="Prov.25.16">Pro 25:16</reference>, he who willingly enjoys, and in 17, he to whom it is given to enjoy without his will; and is not, then, <reference osisRef="Prov.25.16">Pro 25:16</reference> a sentence complete in itself in meaning? That it is not to be understood in a purely dietetic sense (although thus interpreted it is a rule not to be despised), is self-evident. As one can suffer injury from the noblest of food if he overload his stomach therewith, so in the sphere of science, instruction, edification, there is an injurious overloading of the mind; we ought to measure what we receive by our spiritual want, the right distribution of enjoyment and labour, and the degree of our ability to change it <hi type="italic">in succum et sanguinem</hi>, - else it at last awakens in us dislike, and becomes an evil to us.
entries.322ef5e2cf0b9d48474fb6f3c147eeaedfba528e: <reference osisRef="Prov.25.17">Pro 25:17</reference> <div eID="gen11656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11657" type="x-p"/> This proverb is of a kindred character to the foregoing. “If thy comrade eats honey,” says an Arabic proverb quoted by Hitzig, “do not lick it all up.” But the emblem of honey is not continued in this verse: <div eID="gen11657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11658" type="x-p"/> Make rare thy foot in thy neighbour’s house, <div eID="gen11658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11659" type="x-p"/> Lest he be satiated with thee, and hate thee. <div eID="gen11659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11660" type="x-p"/> To make one’s foot rare or dear from a neighbour’s house is equivalent to: to enter it seldom, and not too frequently; הוקר includes in itself the idea of keeping at a distance (Targ. כּלה רגלך; Symmachus, ὑπόστειλον; and another: φίμωσον πόδα σου), and מן has the sense of the Arab. 'an, and is not the comparative, as at <reference osisRef="Isa.13.12">Isa 13:12</reference> : regard thy visit dearer than the house of a neighbour (Heidenheim). The proverb also is significant as to the relation of friend to friend, whose reciprocal love may be turned into hatred by too much intercourse and too great fondness. But רעך is including a friend, any one with whom we stand in any kind of intercourse. “Let him who seeks to be of esteem,” says a German proverb, “come seldom;” and that may be said with reference to him whom his heart draws to another, and also to him who would be of use to another by drawing him out of the false way and guiding on the right path - a showing of esteem, a confirming of love by visiting, should not degenerate into forwardness which appears as burdensome servility, as indiscreet self-enjoyment; nor into a restless impetuosity, which seeks at once to gain by force that which one should allow gradually to ripen. <div eID="gen11660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11661" type="x-p"/> This group of proverbs has the word רע in each of them, connecting them together. The first of the group represents a false tongue:
entries.b45380bd5c781be516a7252114a5a778cf6cfd74: <reference osisRef="Prov.25.18">Pro 25:18</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.25.18">18</reference> A hammer, and a sword, and a sharp arrow -      A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour. <div eID="gen11661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11662" type="x-p"/> An emblematic, or, as we might also say, an iconological proverb; for 18a is a <hi type="italic">quodlibet</hi> of instruments of murder, and 18b is the subscription under it: that which these weapons of murder accomplish, is done to his neighbour by a man who bears false witness against him - he ruins his estate, takes away his honour, but yet more: he murders him, at one time more grossly, at another time with more refinement; at one time slowly, at another time more quickly. מפיץ, from פּוּץ, is equivalent to מפּץ, and מפּץ from נפץ; the Syr. and Targ. have instead פדועא (פדיעא) from פּדע = פּצע; the word פּריעא, on which Hitzig builds a conjecture, is an error of transcription (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Lagarde and Levy). The expression, 18b, is from the decalogue, <reference osisRef="Exod.20.16">Exo 20:16</reference>; Deu 5:17. It is for the most part translated the same here as there: he who speaks against his neighbour as a false witness. But rightly the lxx, Jerome, the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., and Luther: false testimony. As אל sA .y signifies both that which is mighty = power, and Him who is mighty = God, so עד signifies both him who bears testimony and the testimony that is borne, properly that which repeats itself and thereby strengthens itself; accordingly we say ענה עד, to give testimony in reply - viz. to the judge who asks - or generally to offer testimony (even unasked); as well as ענה לעד, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.21">Deu 31:21</reference>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, as evidence (Jerome, <hi type="italic">pro testimonio</hi>). The prep. ב with this ענה has always the meaning of <hi type="italic">contra</hi>, also at <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.3">1Sa 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.30.33">Gen 30:33</reference> is, however, open to question.
entries.f64486570a73307ce7acb518b3547672614c36e4: <reference osisRef="Prov.25.19">Pro 25:19</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.25.19">19</reference> A worthless tooth and an unsteady foot -      Trust in a faithless man in the day of need. <div eID="gen11662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11663" type="x-p"/> The form רעה (with <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> on the antepenult), <reference osisRef="Isa.29.19">Isa 29:19</reference>, takes the place of an <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. <hi type="italic">absol</hi>.; רעה here (about the tone syllable of which <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi> does not decide, thus without doubt <hi type="italic">Milra</hi>) is certainly not a subst.: tooth of breaking (Gesen.); for how strange such a designation of a worthless tooth! שׁן is indeed mas. in <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.5">1Sa 14:5</reference>, but it can also be used as fem., as רגל, which is for the most part fem., also occurs as mas., Göttche. §650. Böttcher, in the new <hi type="italic">Aehrenlese</hi>, and in the Lehrbuch, takes רעה as fem. of an adj. רע, after the form חל; but חל is not an adj., and does not form a fem., although it means not merely profanity, but that which is profane; this is true also of the Aram. חוּל; for חוּלתּא, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.9">Est 2:9</reference>, Targ., is a female name mistaken by Buxtorf. Are we then to read רעה, with Hitzig, after the lxx? - an unimportant change. We interpret the traditional רעה, with Fleischer, as derived from רועעה, from רועע, breaking to pieces (crumbling), in an intransitive sense. The form מוּעדת is also difficult. Böttcher regards it as also, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Aben Ezra after the example of Gecatilia as <hi type="italic">part</hi>. <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>. = מועדת, “only on account of the pausal tone and the combination of the two letters מע with <hi type="italic">û</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">ô</hi>.” But this vocal change, with its reasons, is merely imaginary. מוּעדת is the <hi type="italic">part. Pual</hi>, with the preformative מ struck out, Ewald 169d. The objection that the <hi type="italic">part. Pual</hi> should be ממעד, after the form מבער, does not prove anything to the contrary; for מועדת cannot be the fem. so as not to coincide with the fem. of the <hi type="italic">part</hi>. <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, cf. besides to the long <hi type="italic">û</hi> the form without the <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> יוּקשׁים, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.12">Ecc 9:12</reference> = מיקּשׁים (Arnheim, <hi type="italic">Gramm</hi>. p. 139). רגל מוּעדת is a leg that has become tottering, trembling. He who in a time of need makes a faithless man his ground of confidence, is like one who seeks to bite with a broken tooth, and which he finally crushes, and one who supports himself on a shaking leg, and thus stumbles and falls. The gen. connection מבטח בוגד signifies either the ground of confidence consisting in a faithless man, or the confidence placed in one who is faithless. But, after the Masora, we are to read here, as at <reference osisRef="Ps.65.6">Psa 65:6</reference>, מבטח, which <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 184a also confirms, and as it is also found in the Venice 1525, Basel 1619, and in Norzi. This מבטה is constr. according to Kimchi, notwithstanding the <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi>; as also משׁקל, Ezr 8:30 (after Abulwalîd, Kimchi, and Norzi). In this passage before us, מבטח בוגד may signify a deceitful ground of confidence (cf. <reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Hab 2:5</reference>), but the two other passages present a genit. connection of the words. We must thus suppose that the ā of מבטח and משׁקל, in these three passages, is regarded as fixed, like the <hi type="italic">â</hi> of the form (Arab.) mif'âl.
entries.4393d1df26666a4582d1c00ab682797d25ace1da: <reference osisRef="Prov.25.20">Pro 25:20</reference> <div eID="gen11663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11664" type="x-p"/> The above proverb, which connects itself with <reference osisRef="Prov.25.18">Pro 25:18</reference>, not only by the sound רע, but also by שׁן, which is assonant with שׁנון, is followed by another with the catchword רע: 20 He that layeth aside his coat on a day of frost, vinegar on nitre,      And he who welcomes with songs a dejected heart. <div eID="gen11664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11665" type="x-p"/> Is not this intelligible, sensible, ingenious? All these three things are wrong. The first is as wrong as the second, and the third, which the proverb has in view, is morally wrong, for one ought to weep with those that weep, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.15">Rom 12:15</reference>; he, on the contrary, who laughs among those who weep, is, on the most favourable judgment, a fool. That which is wrong in 20a, according to Böttcher in the <hi type="italic">Aehrenlese</hi>, 1849, consists in this, that one in severe cold puts on a fine garment. As if there were not garments which are at the same time beautiful, and keep warm? In the new <hi type="italic">Aehrenlese</hi> he prefers the reading משׁנּה: if one changes his coat. But that surely he might well enough do, if the one were warmer than the other! Is it then impossible that מעדה, in the connection, means <hi type="italic">transire faciens</hi> = <hi type="italic">removens</hi>? The <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> עדה, <hi type="italic">tarnsiit</hi>, occurs at Job 28:8. So also, in the poetic style. העדה might be used in the sense of the Aram. אעדּי. Rightly Aquila, Symmachus, περιαιρῶν; the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. better, ἀφαιρούμενος (Mid.). בּגד is an overcoat or mantle, so called from covering, as לבוּשׁ (R. לב, to fasten, fix), the garment lying next the body, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Psa 22:19. Thus, as it is foolish to lay off upper clothing on a frosty day, so it is foolish also to pour vinegar on nitre; carbonic acid nitre, whether it be mineral (which may be here thought of) or vegetable, is dissolved in water, and serves diverse purposes (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Isa.1.25">Isa 1:25</reference>); but if one pours vinegar on it, it is destroyed. לב־רע<note placement="foot">The writing wavers between על לב־רע (cf. על עם־דּל) and על־בל רע dna )על ע.</note> is, at <reference osisRef="Prov.26.23">Pro 26:23</reference> and elsewhere, a heart morally bad, here a heart badly disposed, one inclined to that which is evil; for שׁר שׁיר is the contrast of קונן קינה, and always the consequence of a disposition joyfully excited; the inconsistency lies in this, that one thinks to cheer a sorrowful heart by merry singing, if the singing has an object, and is not much more the reckless expression of an animated pleasure in view of the sad condition of another. שׁיר על .rehtona  signifies, as at <reference osisRef="Job.33.27">Job 33:27</reference>, to sing to any one, to address him in singing; cf. דּבּר על, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.10">Jer 6:10</reference>, and particularly על־לב, Hos 2:16; Isa 40:2. The ב of בּשּׁרים is neither the partitive, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.5">Pro 9:5</reference>, nor the transitive, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.30">Pro 20:30</reference>, but the instrumental; for, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Exod.7.20">Exo 7:20</reference>, the obj. of the action is thought of as its means (Gesen. §138, Anm. 3*); one sings “with songs,” for definite songs underlie his singing. The lxx, which the Syr., Targ., and Jerome more or less follow, has formed from this proverb one quite different: “As vinegar is hurtful to a wound, so an injury to the body makes the heart sorrowful; as the moth in clothes, and the worm in wood, so the sorrow of a man injures his heart.” The wisdom of this pair of proverbs is not worth much, and after all inquiry little or nothing comes of it. The Targ. at least preserves the figure 20b: as he who pours vinegar (Syr. chalo) on nitre; the Peshito, however, and here and there also the Targum, has jathro (arrow-string) instead of methro (nitre). Hitzig adopts this, and changes the tristich into the distich: <div eID="gen11665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11666" type="x-p"/> He that meeteth archers with arrow on the string, <div eID="gen11666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11667" type="x-p"/> Is like him who singeth songs with a sad heart. <div eID="gen11667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11668" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew of this proverb of Hitzig’s (מרים קרה על־יתר) is unhebraic, the meaning dark as an oracle, and its moral contents nil.
entries.8c4f32076c8bdd4d93008fa607e4626e113f24c9: <reference osisRef="Prov.25.21-Prov.22.21">Pro 25:21-22 21</reference> If thine enemy hunger, feed him with bread;      And if he thirst, give him water to drink. 22 For thereby thou heapest burning coals on his head,      And Jahve will recompense it to thee. <div eID="gen11668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11669" type="x-p"/> The translation of this proverb by the lxx is without fault; Paul cites therefrom Rom 12:20. The participial construction of 22a, the lxx, rightly estimating it, thus renders: for, doing this, thou shalt heap coals on his head. The expression, “thou shalt heap” (σωρεύσεις), is also appropriate; for חתה certainly means first only to fetch or bring fire (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.6.27">Pro 6:27</reference>); but here, by virtue of the <hi type="italic">constructio praegnans</hi> with על, to fetch, and hence to heap up - to pile upon. Burning pain, as commonly observed, is the figure of burning shame, on account of undeserved kindness shown by an enemy (Fleischer). But how burning coals heaped on the head can denote burning shame, is not to be perceived, for the latter is a burning on the cheeks; wherefore Hitzig and Rosenmüller explain: thou wilt thus bring on him the greatest pain, and appease thy vengeance, while at the same time Jahve will reward thy generosity. Now we say, indeed, that he who rewards evil with good takes the noblest revenge; but if this doing of good proceed from a revengeful aim, and is intended sensibly to humble an adversary, then it loses all its moral worth, and is changed into selfish, malicious wickedness. Must the proverb then be understood in this ignoble sense? The Scriptures elsewhere say that guilt and punishment are laid on the head of any one when he is made to experience and to bear them. Chrysostom and others therefore explain after <reference osisRef="Ps.140.10">Psa 140:10</reference> and similar passages, but thereby the proverb is morally falsified, and <reference osisRef="Prov.25.22">Pro 25:22</reference> accords with <reference osisRef="Prov.25.21">Pro 25:21</reference>, which counsels not to the avenging of oneself, but to the requital of evil with good. The burning of coals laid on the head must be a painful but wholesome consequence; it is a figure of self-accusing repentance (Augustine, Zöckler), for the producing of which the showing of good to an enemy is a noble motive. That God rewards such magnanimity may not be the special motive; but this view might contribute to it, for otherwise such promises of God as <reference osisRef="Isa.58.8-Isa.58.12">Isa 58:8-12</reference> were without moral right. The proverb also requires one to show himself gentle and liberal toward a needy enemy, and present a twofold reason for this: first, that thereby his injustice is brought home to his conscience; and, secondly, that thus God is well-pleased in such practical love toward an enemy, and will reward it; - by such conduct, apart from the performance of a law grounded in our moral nature, one advances the happiness of his neighbour and his own.
entries.b7ab347081d28031a0ebeaa24ce656bc7df43519: <reference osisRef="Prov.25.23">Pro 25:23</reference> <div eID="gen11669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11670" type="x-p"/> The next group of proverbs extends from <reference osisRef="Prov.25.23">Pro 25:23</reference> to Pro 25:28. 23 Wind from the north produceth rain;      And a secret tongue a troubled countenance. <div eID="gen11670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11671" type="x-p"/> The north is called צפון, from צפן, to conceal, from the firmament darkening itself for a longer time, and more easily, like the old Persian apâkhtara, as (so it appears) the starless, and, like <hi type="italic">aquilo</hi>, the north wind, as bringing forward the black clouds. But properly the “fathers of rain” are, in Syria, the west and the south-west; and so little can צפון here mean the pure north wind, that Jerome, who knew from his own experience the changes of weather in Palestine, helps himself, after Symmachus (διαλύει βροχήν), with a <hi type="italic">quid pro quo</hi> out of the difficulty: <hi type="italic">ventus aquilo dissipat pluvias</hi>; the Jewish interpreters (Aben Ezra, Joseph Kimchi, and Meîri) also thus explain, for they connect together תחולל, in the meaning תמנע, with the unintelligible חלילה (far be it!). But צפון may also, perhaps like ζόφος (<hi type="italic">Deutsch. Morgenl. Zeitsch</hi>. xxi. 600f.), standing not without connection therewith, denote the northwest; and probably the proverb emphasized the northern direction of the compass, because, according to the intention of the similitude, he seeks to designate such rain as is associated with raw, icy-cold weather, as the north wind (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.16">Pro 27:16</reference>, lxx, Sir. 43:20) brings along with it. The names of the winds are <hi type="italic">gen. fem</hi>., <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Isa 43:6. תּחולל (Aquila, ὠδίνει; cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.8.24">Pro 8:24</reference>, ὠδινήθην) has in Codd., <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the <hi type="italic">Jaman</hi>., the tone on the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>., and with <hi type="italic">Tsere</hi> <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> (<hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi>, p. 21) serving as העמדה. So also the Arab. nataj is used of the wind, as helping the birth of the rain-clouds. Manifestly פנים נזעמים, countenances manifesting extreme displeasure (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> זעם, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.24">Pro 24:24</reference>), are compared to rain. With justice Hitzig renders פנים, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Joh 2:6, in the plur. sense; because, for the influence which the tongue slandering in secret (<reference osisRef="Ps.101.5">Psa 101:5</reference>) has on the slandered, the “sorrowful countenance” would not be so characteristic as for the influence which it exercises on the mutual relationships of men: the secret babbler, the confidential communication throwing suspicion, now on this one and now on that one, behind their backs, excites men against one another, so that one shows to another a countenance in which deep displeasure and suspicion express themselves.
entries.320ffe9f6b8d833f8666d2530daad26e12bbad07: <reference osisRef="Prov.25.24">Pro 25:24</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.25.24">24</reference> Better to sit on the top of a roof,      Than a quarrelsome woman and a house in common. <div eID="gen11671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11672" type="x-p"/> A repetition of Pro 21:9.
entries.2019ff117beceb8c85eccbce77dac17117114897: <reference osisRef="Prov.25.25">Pro 25:25</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.25.25">25</reference> Fresh water to a thirsty soul;      And good news from a far country.<hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., regarding the form of this proverb, vol. i. p. 9; we have a similar proverb regarding the influence of good news at Pro 15:30. Fresh cold water is called at <reference osisRef="Jer.18.14">Jer 18:14</reference> מים קרים; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding קר, 18:27. “עיף, cogn. יעף, and עוּף, properly to become darkened, therefore figuratively like (Arab.) gushiya 'alyh, to become faint, to become feeble unto death, of the darkness which spreads itself over the eyes” (Fleischer). <div eID="gen11672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11673" type="x-p"/> This proverb, with the figure of “fresh water,” is now followed by one with the figure of a “fountain”:
entries.52a8ce1be54c11d756695bff89b62f29ac493c55: <reference osisRef="Prov.25.26">Pro 25:26</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.25.26">26</reference> A troubled fountain and a ruined spring -      A righteous man yielding to a godless man. <div eID="gen11673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11674" type="x-p"/> For the most part, in מט one thinks of a yielding in consequence of being forced. Thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Fleischer: as a troubled ruined spring is a misfortune for the people who drink out of it, or draw from it, so is it a misfortune for the surrounding of the righteous, when he is driven from his dwelling or his possession by an unrighteous man. And it is true: the righteous can be compared to a well (מעין, well-spring, from עין, a well, as an eye of the earth, and מקור, fountain, from קוּר, R. קר, כר, to round out, to dig out), with reference to the blessing which flows from it to its surroundings (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.10.11">Pro 10:11</reference> and Joh 7:38). But the words “yielding to” (contrast “stood before,” 2Ki 10:4, or <reference osisRef="Josh.7.12">Jos 7:12</reference>), in the phrase “yielding to the godless,” may be understood of a spontaneous as well as of a constrained, forced, wavering and yielding, as the expression in the Psalm בּל־אמּוט [<hi type="italic">non movebor</hi>, Psa 10:6] affirms the certainty of being neither inwardly nor outwardly ever moved or shaken. The righteous shall stand fast and strong in God without fearing the godless (Isa 51:12.), unmoveable and firm as a brazen wall (Jer 1:17.). If, however, he is wearied with resistance, and from the fear of man, or the desire to please man, or from a false love of peace he yields before it, and so gives way - then he becomes like to a troubled fountain (רפשׂ, cogn. רמס, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.18">Eze 34:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.25">Isa 41:25</reference>; Jerome: <hi type="italic">fans turbatus pede</hi>), a ruined spring; his character, hitherto pure, is now corrupted by his own guilt, and now far from being a blessing to others, his wavering is a cause of sorrow to the righteous, and an offence to the weak - he is useful no longer, but only injurious. Rightly Lagarde: “The verse, one of the most profound of the whole book, does not speak of the misfortunate, but of the fall of the righteous, whose sin compromises the holy cause which he serves, 2Sa 12:14.” Thus also <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Löwenstein, with reference to the proverb <hi type="italic">Sanhedrin </hi>92b: also in the time of danger let not a man disown his honour. Bachja, in his <hi type="italic">Ethics</hi>, referring to this figure, 26a, thinks of the possibility of restoration: the righteous wavers only for the moment, but at last he comes right (מתמוטט ועולה). But this interpretation of the figure destroys the point of the proverb.
entries.671c04498ba4decef295f6d8fd89d4986d8a1420: <reference osisRef="Prov.25.27">Pro 25:27</reference> <div eID="gen11674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11675" type="x-p"/> This verse, as it stands, is scarcely to be understood. The <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. translates 27b literally: ἔρευνά τε δόξας αὐτῶν δόξα; but what is the reference of this כּבדם? Euchel and others refer it to men, for they translate: “to set a limit to the glory of man is true glory;” but the “glory of man” is denoted by the phrase כּבד אדם, not by כּבדם; and, besides, חקר does not mean measure and limit. Oetinger explains: “To eat too much honey is not good; whereas the searching after their glory, viz., of pleasant and praiseworthy things, which are likened to honey, is glory, cannot be too much done, and is never without utility and honour;” but how can כּבדם be of the same meaning as כּבד הדברים אשׁר or הנמשׁלים כּדּבשׁ - such an abbreviation of the expression is impossible. Schultens, according to Rashi: <hi type="italic">vestigatio gravitatis eorum est gravitas</hi>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the searching out of their difficulty is a trouble; better Vitringa (since כבוד nowhere occurs in this sense of <hi type="italic">gravitas molesta ac pondere oppressura</hi>): <hi type="italic">investigatio praestantiae eorum est gloriosa</hi>; but Vitringa, in order to gain a connection to 27a, needs to introduce <hi type="italic">etiamsi</hi>, and in both explanations the reference of the כּבדם is imaginary, and it by no means lies near, since the Scripture uses the word כבוד of God, and His kingdom and name, but never of His law or His revelation. Thus also is an argument against Bertheau, who translates: the searching out of their glory (viz., of the divine law and revelation) is a burden, a strenuous occupation of the mind, since חקר does not in itself mean searching out, and is equivocally, even unintelligibly, expressed, since כבוד denotes, it is true, here and there, a great multitude, but never a burden (as כּבד). The thought which Jerome finds in 27b: <hi type="italic">qui scrutator est majestatis opprimetur a gloria</hi>, is judicious, and connects itself synonym. with 27a; but such a thought is unwarranted, for he disregards the suff. of כּבדם, and renders כבוד in the sense of difficulty (oppression). Or should it perhaps be vocalized כּבדם (Syr., Targ., Theodotion, δεδοξασμένα = נכבּדות)? Thus vocalized, Umbreit renders it in the sense of <hi type="italic">honores</hi>; Elster and Zöckler in the sense of <hi type="italic">difficultates</hi> (<hi type="italic">difficilia</hi>); but this plur., neither the biblical, nor, so far as I know, the post-bibl. usage of the word has ever adopted. However, the sense of the proverb which Elster and Zöckler gain is certainly that which is aimed at. We accordingly translate: <div eID="gen11675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11676" type="x-p"/> To surfeit oneself in eating honey is not good, <div eID="gen11676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11677" type="x-p"/> But as an inquirer to enter on what is difficult is honour. <div eID="gen11677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11678" type="x-p"/> We read כּבדם instead of כּבדם. This change commends itself far more than כּבד מכּבוד (וחקר), according to which Gesenius explains: <hi type="italic">nimium studium honoris est sine honore</hi> - impossible, for חקר does not signify <hi type="italic">nimium studium</hi>, in the sense of striving, but only that of inquiry: one strives after honour, but does not study it. Hitzig and Ewald, after the example of J. D. Michaelis, Arnoldi, and Ziegler, betake themselves therefore to the Arabic; Ewald explains, for he leaves the text unchanged: “To despise their honour (that is, of men) is honour (true, real honour);” Hitzig, for he changes the text like Gesenius: “To despise honour is more than honour,” with the ingenious remark: To obtain an order [<hi type="italic">insigne ordinis</hi>] is an honour, but not to wear it then for the first time is its bouquet. Nowhere any trace either in Hebrew or in Aramaic is to be found of the verb חקר, to despise (to be despised), and so it must here remain without example.<note placement="foot">The Hebrew meaning <hi type="italic">investigare</hi>, and the equivalent Arabic ḥaḳr, <hi type="italic">contemnere</hi> (<hi type="italic">contemtui esse</hi>), are derivations from the primary meaning (R. חק): to go down from above firmly on anything, and thus to press in (to cut in), or also to press downward.</note> <div eID="gen11678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11679" type="x-p"/> Nor have we any need of it. The change of כּבדם into כּבדם is enough. The proverb is an antithetic distich; 27a warns against inordinate longing after enjoyments, 27b praises earnest labour. Instead of דּבשׁ הרבּות, if honey in the mass were intended, the words would have been דּבשׁ הרבּה (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.11">Ecc 5:11</reference>; 1Ki 10:10), or at least הרבּות דּבשׁ (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.9">Amo 4:9</reference>); הרבות can only be a <hi type="italic">n. actionis</hi>, and אכל דּבשׁ its inverted object (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.9.4">Jer 9:4</reference>), as Böttcher has discerned: to make much of the eating of honey, to do much therein is not good (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.25.16">Pro 25:16</reference>). In 27b Luther also partly hits on the correct rendering: “and he who searches into difficult things, to him it is too difficult,” for which it ought to be said: to him it is an honour. כּבדם, viz., דברים, signifies difficult things, as ריקים, <reference osisRef="Prov.12.11">Pro 12:11</reference>, vain things. The Heb. כּבד, however, never means difficult to be understood or comprehended (although more modern lexicons say this),<note placement="foot">Cf. Sir. 3:20f. with Ben-Sira’s Heb. text in my <hi type="italic">Gesch. der jüd. Poesie</hi>, p. 204 (vv. 30-32); nowhere does this adj. כבד appears here in this warning against meditating over the transcendental.</note> but always only burdensome and heavy, <hi type="italic">gravis</hi>, not <hi type="italic">difficilis</hi>. כבדם are also things of which the חקר, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the fundamental searching into them (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.17">Pro 18:17</reference>; Pro 25:2.), costs an earnest effort, which perhaps, according to the first impression, appears to surpass the available strength (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.18.18">Exo 18:18</reference>). To overdo oneself in eating honey is not good; on the contrary, the searching into difficult subjects is nothing less than an eating of honey, but an honour. There is here a <hi type="italic">paronomasia</hi>. Fleischer translates it: <hi type="italic">explorare gravia grave est</hi>; but we render <hi type="italic">grave est</hi> not in the sense of <hi type="italic">molestiam creat</hi>, but <hi type="italic">gravitatem parit</hi> (weight = respect, honour).
entries.57ddc8fbee62408d81749a2b329ffec4c31d12ae: <reference osisRef="Prov.25.28">Pro 25:28</reference> <div eID="gen11679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11680" type="x-p"/> This verse, counselling restraint as to the spirit, is connected with the foregoing, which counsels to self-control as to enjoyment: <div eID="gen11680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11681" type="x-p"/> A city broken through, now without walls - <div eID="gen11681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11682" type="x-p"/> A man without self-control over his spirit. <div eID="gen11682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11683" type="x-p"/> A “city broken down” is one whose wall is “broken,” <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.5">2Ch 32:5</reference>, whether it has met with breaches (פּרצים), or is wholly broken; in the former case also the city is incapable of being defended, and it is all one as if it had no wall. Such a city is like a man “who hath no control over his own spirit” (for the accentuation of the Heb. words here, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi>, p. 10): <hi type="italic">cujus spiritui nulla cohibitio</hi> (Schultens), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, <hi type="italic">qui animum suum cohibere non potest</hi> (Fleischer: עצר, R. צר, to press together, to oppress, and thereby to hold back). As such a city can be plundered and laid waste without trouble, so a man who knows not to hold in check his desires and affections is in constant danger of blindly following the impulse of his unbridled sensuality, and of being hurried forward to outbreaks of passion, and thus of bringing unhappiness upon himself. There are sensual passions (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, drunkenness), intellectual (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, ambition), mingled (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, revenge); but in all of these a false ego rules, which, instead of being held down by the true and better ego, rises to unbounded supremacy.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Drbal’s <hi type="italic">Empirische Psychologie</hi>, §137.</note> <div eID="gen11683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11684" type="x-p"/> Therefore the expression used is not לנפשׁו, but לרוּחו; desire has its seat in the soul, but in the spirit it grows into passion, which in the root of all its diversities is selfishness (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 199); self-control is accordingly the ruling of the spirit, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the restraining (keeping down) of the false enslaved ego-life by the true and free, and powerful in God Himself.  <chapter eID="Prov.25"/> <div eID="gen11684" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="1">1 THese <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Which are contain'd in this and the following Chapters.</ns0:note>

                  <ns0:p n="2">2 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 29. 29. Rom. 11. 33.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>It is</ns0:hi> the glory of God <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">It is agreeable to the Nature, and highly conducing to the Honour of God, because it is a Testimony of his infinite Wisdom and Knowledg, of his absolute Power and Soveraignty, and of his other incomprehensible Perfections.</ns0:note> to conceal a thing <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">To keep his counsels, and the reasons of his actions in his own Breast, that he needs not to im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />part them to any other for their advice and assistance, as being self-sufficient both for the contrivance and execution of whatsoever pleaseth him, and accountable to none for any of his matters.</ns0:note>: but the honour of kings <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">But Kings must not affect to be like God in this respect, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause they are Creatures, and therefore ignorant and insufficient, and accountable to an higher Authority.</ns0:note> to search out a matter <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">In the conduct of their great affairs, not to lean to their own understandings, nor to be wedded to their own wills, but to communicate their counsels to others, that so they may search and find out the true and right way, and to be ready to give a satisfactory account of the Justice and reasonableness of them as occasion shall require.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 The heaven for height, and the earth for depth <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">As no Man upon Earth can exactly discover the height of Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven, or the depth of Earth, or discern what is contained in them.</ns0:note>, and the heart of kings <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. there is <ns0:hi>no searching.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> unsearchable <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Though wise Kings will search out other men and things, yet their inward thoughts and purposes are hardly discoverable, part<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly because every Man's Heart lies out of the fight of others, and partly because it is the practice of Kings industriously to conceal their intentions.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Take away the dross from the silver, and there shall come forth a vessel for the finer <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Then, and not till then it is fit for that use.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 20. 8.</ns0:note> Take away the wicked <ns0:hi>from</ns0:hi> before the king <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">From his Court and Councels.</ns0:note>, and his throne shall be established <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">By removing them who by their wicked counsels and practices provoked God's displeasure against the King, and blasted his Reputation, and alienated the Hearts of his People from him.</ns0:note> in righteous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">By such impartial execution of Justice.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> set not out thy glory.</ns0:note> Put not forth thy self <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>Do not magnifie,</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>glorifie thy self,</ns0:hi> by vaunting speech or carriage, but, which is implied, carry thy self humbly and mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />destly, which is most pleasing to Kings, and most becoming and safe for thee.</ns0:note> in the presence of the king, and stand not in the place of great <ns0:hi>men</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Do not affect nor use frequent and familiar Society with greater Persons than thy self, whereby thou maist easily involve thy self in much guilt, and expose thy self to envy or contempt, and to many other inconveniences.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luk. 14. 10.</ns0:note> For better <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">It is more for thy credit and comfort.</ns0:note> that it be said unto thee <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">By some publick Officer<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> or by the King himself.</ns0:note>, Come up hither: than that thou shouldst be put lower in the presence of the prince whom thine eyes have seen <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Into whose presence and ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quaintance thou hast so boldly intruded thy self, who as before he observed thy impudence so now he sees and suffers this publick dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />grace to be cast upon thee.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 Go not forth hastily <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Without necessary cause and due consideration.</ns0:note> to strive <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Either ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dicially or otherwise.</ns0:note>, lest <ns0:hi>thou know not</ns0:hi> what to do in the end thereof, when thy neighbour hath put thee to shame <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">For thy folly in undertaking what thou wast not able to accomplish, and for thy injustice in charging him wrongfully.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="12">12 <ns0:hi>As</ns0:hi> an ear-ring of Gold, and ornament of fine gold <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Highly acceptable and a great Ornament, and not an offence<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and dishonour, as fools esteem it.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>so is</ns0:hi> a wise reprover <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">That reproves an offender faithfully. Or 2. as a cool Air such as is in Snowy seasons. Or 3. as drink which is as cold as Snow.</ns0:note> in the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>day.</ns0:hi> Gen. 2. 4.</ns0:note> time of harvest, <ns0:hi>so</ns0:hi> is a faithful messenger to them that send him: for he <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">

                     </ns0:note> refresheth the soul of his masters <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">With a true account and speedy dispatch of those important Affairs which were committed to him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 Whoso boasteth himself <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">

                        </ns0:gap> of falshood.</ns0:note> of a false gift <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Pretending that he hath given, or promising that he will give a Man those gifts, which he neither hath given, nor intendeth to give him.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>is like</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jude 12.</ns0:note> clouds and wind without rain <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Like empty Clouds carried about with wind, and not affording that Rain which by their appearance they pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mise.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 32. 4. & 1 Sam. 25. 24. & Ch. 15. 1. & 16. 14.</ns0:note> By long forbearing <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">By patient submission and expectation.</ns0:note> is a prince persuaded <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>pacified,</ns0:hi> whereas his rage is increased by opposition. Compare <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 10. 4.</ns0:note>, and a soft tongue <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">A mild and humble answer.</ns0:note> breaketh the bone <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Softneth an Heart which is as hard as Bone or Stone. He alludes to those Oyls which sink through the Flesh to the very Bone. See <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 109. 18.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Vers. 27.</ns0:note> Hast thou found honey <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Which in those parts was oft found in Woods or Fields, as <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 14. 8, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 14. 25. By <ns0:hi>Honey</ns0:hi> he understands, not onely all delicious Meats, but all present and worldly delights, which we are here taught to use with moderation,</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">onely.</ns0:note> eat so much as is sufficient for thee, lest thou be filled therewith, and vo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mit it <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Hony ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessively taken disposeth a Man to vomiting.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                        </ns0:gap> foot be seldom in thy neigh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bours house.</ns0:note> Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbours house <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Visit him not too frequently nor unseasonably.</ns0:note>, lest he be <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> full of thee.</ns0:note> weary of thee, and <ns0:hi>so</ns0:hi> hate thee <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">As men are apt to loath those Meats of which they surfeit, as was now observed, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 16.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 120. 3, 4. Ch. 12. 18.</ns0:note> A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour, <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a maul, and a sword, and a sharp ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />row <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Is as cruel and pernicious to him as any instrument of Death<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> The design of the Proverb is to shew the wickedness of slander, and that a false witness is in some respect as bad as a Mur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derer.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:537" />19 Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble, <ns0:hi>is like</ns0:hi> a broken tooth and a foot out of joynt <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">It is not onely deceitful, but hurtful, as a broken Tooth though it make shew of helping, yet is not onely unhelpful to a Man for chewing his Meat, but also troublesome and painful; and as a Foot out of Joynt, doth not help but hinder, and pain him that attempts to walk upon it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 <ns0:hi>As</ns0:hi> he that taketh away a garment in cold wea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">When it is most seasonable and necessary.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and as</ns0:hi> vinegar upon nitre <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Which dissolves the Nitre, and makes it useless and ineffectual.</ns0:note>; so <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> he <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">He is no less absurd and impertinent.</ns0:note> that singeth songs to an heavy heart <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Whose grief is not relieved but in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />creased by it, as common experience sheweth, and divers learned Authors have observed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                        </ns0:gap> 12. 20.</ns0:note> If thine enemy be hungry, give him Bread <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>Bread</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Water</ns0:hi> he understands all things necessary for his subsistence.</ns0:note> to eat: and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 For <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Understand, <ns0:hi>in so doing,</ns0:hi> which words are expressed, <ns0:hi>Rom</ns0:hi> 12. 20. where this Text is quoted.</ns0:note> thou shalt heap <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 11. 6. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 10.</ns0:note> coals of fire upon his head <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Either 1. in a bad sense, Thou shalt hereby aggravate his sin and occasion a more speedy and grie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vous vengeance from God, which, like fire from Heaven, shall fall upon his Head and consume him. Not that he persuades him to do a kindness with an evil intent, with an expectation or desire, or design of bringing God's wrath upon him, but onely he foretels what would happen and dissuades him from taking vengeance, and provokes him to kindness instead of it, because vengeance is God's peculiar work which he will certainly inflict upon such Persons, which argument is used to that very purpose by St. <ns0:hi>Paul, Rom.</ns0:hi> 12. 19. Or 2. in a good sense, Thou shalt melt him into repen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tance and inflame him with love and kindness to thee for so un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />expected and undeserved a favour, he shall be as neartily grie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved and tormented with the Thoughts of his vile and wicked carriage to thee, as a Man would <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e that had burning Coals of Fire heaped upon his Head. But if these Coals of Fire do not melt him but still he hardens his Heart against thee, they will consume him. Thus either by the one or by the other way thou shall be secured and deliverd from him. The Metaphor may seem to be taken from Founders who melt the hardest Metals by heaping Coals of Fire upon them. And <ns0:hi>the Head</ns0:hi> may be here mentioned rather than any other part, because in Scripture Phrase both Blessings and Curses are said to fall upon mens Heads, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> upon them, <ns0:hi>heads</ns0:hi> being frequently put for Persons.</ns0:note>, and the LORD shall reward thee <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Thy charity to him shall be fully recompensed to thee, if not by him, yet by God, which is far better.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                     </ns0:note> The North-wind driveth away rain: so <ns0:hi>doth</ns0:hi> an angry countenance <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">In the hearer, who by his countenance sheweth his dislike of such Persons and practices.</ns0:note> a backbiting tongue <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>a secret Tongue,</ns0:hi> which <ns0:hi>privily slandereth his Neighbour</ns0:hi> as it is expressed, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 101. 5. and as the man<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner of Back-biters is. But this Verse is otherwise rendred in the Margent, and by diverse others, <ns0:hi>The North Wind bringeth forth</ns0:hi> (as this Verb properly and most frequently signifies, and as it is rendred by all the Ancient Interpreters, and by many others) <ns0:hi>Rain:</ns0:hi> (which it doth in <ns0:hi>Iudea,</ns0:hi> because the Sea lies Norward, as well as West<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward, from it, as also in <ns0:hi>Africa,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Aristotle</ns0:hi> observes, though it drive away Rain in Countries of another situation) <ns0:hi>so doth a backbiting Tongue</ns0:hi> (cause) <ns0:hi>an angry Countenance,</ns0:hi> it causeth much an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ger and mischief, both to the Person slandered, and to the slan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derer, and to other Persons who may be concerned with or for either of them, as is manifest from common experience.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                        </ns0:gap> 8. 19.</ns0:note> It is better to dwell in a corner of the house top, than with a brawling woman and in a wide house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 <ns0:hi>As</ns0:hi> cold waters to a thirsty soul, <ns0:hi>so is</ns0:hi> good news from a far countrey <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Because it comes thither more rarely and difficultly, after it hath been long expected and earnestly desired, all which circum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stances make it more acceptable.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 A righteous man falling down <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Either 1. into sin. So the sense is, When a just Man is ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther allured or terrified into any sinful practice before wicked men, or into any base and servile compliance with their Lusts, he who by his excellent counsels was like a Fountain or <ns0:hi>well of life,</ns0:hi> as his Mouth is called, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 10. 11. sending forth refreshing streams for the benefit of many, is now corrupted and rendered unserviceable. Or rather 2. into misery, of which kind of falling this word is con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stantly used, and never to my remembrance of falling into sin. And so the sense is this, When righteous men are oppressed and devoured by the wicked, the state of that Commonwealth is as de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plorable, as if the publick Fountains, from whence all the People fetch their Water, were corrupted, and it is a sign that the Foun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tains of Justice are poisoned.</ns0:note> before the wick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, <ns0:hi>is as</ns0:hi> a troubled fountain, and a corrupt spring.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 * <ns0:hi>It is</ns0:hi> not good <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">To wit, for the health of the Body.</ns0:note> to eat much honey; so <ns0:hi>for men</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Which words are easily understood both out of the foregoing clause, where the Ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ney is supposed to be eaten by men, and out of the following words which are evidently meant of them.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note place="margin">Vers. 16.</ns0:note> to search their own glory <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Industriously to seek for honour and applause from men.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>is not</ns0:hi> glory <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Is not onely sinful, but shame<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful also and a sign of a vain and mean spirit. The Negative Par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticle, <ns0:hi>not</ns0:hi> is here understood out of the former part of the Verse, as it is, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 1. 5. & 9. 18.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
